name: Agwara Kambari / Cishingini
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Stark, Janie P. 2010. Kambari Orthography Design. SIL e-Books 16. Dallas: SIL International. xiv+227 pp. (revision of Stark 2000 PhD, University of Ilorin; covers Agwara Kambari = Cishingini asg, Salka Kambari = Tsishingini tsw, Auna Kambari = Tsikimba kdl)
catalog_locator: sec. 2.3.1.5 'Tone patterns' pp. 61-63; sec. 3.3.2.3 'How to write tone' p. 98; Appendix B Agwara Kambari orthography, 'Tone', p. 192; sec. 2.3.1.4 'Syllable and word patterns' pp. 59-61
catalog_quote: [p. 98, sec. 3.3.2.3] Kambari is tonal, like most African languages, though the burden of comprehension based on tone contrast is slight (see section 2.3.1.5). [p. 61, sec. 2.3.1.5] Lexical tone is demonstrated by pairs of words that differ only in their tonal value. Lexical tone in Kambari carries a very small semantic load. The following tone data indicates Kambari utilizes two level lexical tones. All the examples are in Auna Kambari, but the patterns are the same in the other two languages unless otherwise noted. [p. 63, 'Tone processes'] There are no semantic elements represented by tone alone. [p. 192, Appendix B, Agwara Kambari orthography, 'Tone'] Agwara Kambari has a small number of minimal tone pairs (under 20). Most of the minimal pairs are in different domains, so there is little possibility of confusion when reading. For example ci'in [cíʔin] 'clay' and ci'in [cìʔin] 'intestines'. ... Reader tests of tone in marked and unmarked texts have shown that no information is lost with the unmarked texts.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kambari (including Agwara Kambari = Cishingini asg) is described as a two-level-tone language with a light lexical tone load; the source gives noun and verb tone patterns but makes no statement at all about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone notes: Salka Kambari (tsw) has no word-initial H; imperative verbs nearly always LH with a few LL exceptions; Auna appendix (kdl) p. 200 notes a root-final vowel reduced to /u/ before suffixes that 'does not receive the same length and importance' (headed 'Unstressed /u/'), not a word-stress rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone data elicited on isolated words (citation form of verbs = imperative); statements are for the Kambari cluster generally with Auna examples, plus an Agwara-specific tone paragraph.
new_statements.identity_note: cish1238 / ISO asg = Agwara (West) Kambari, called 'Cishingini' by Stark/KLP/Ethnologue and 'tsuWənci (Ngwunci)' by Blench & McGill 2012, spoken around Agwara west of Lake Kainji (Niger/Kebbi States, into Benin). Beware the name clash: Crozier 1984's 'Cishingini' and Hoffmann's 'Central Kambari' are the SALKA lect = Tsishingini tsw / tsis1238, and the Crozier page in Hartell 1993 (filed by Rosetta under asg) is also Salka. Stark 2010's general phonology statements cover all three KLP lects (Agwara asg, Salka tsw, Auna kdl) with Auna examples; the p. 192 tone paragraph is Agwara-specific.

tone_statements.quote: m̀bókí ánáké cìndèrè I stole 7 cows ... transition tone. ... Pèshè ù cínə́n tə̀ ... → sort of sounds downstepped ... could min pair. méní kàcí kávə̀ I see myself / méní kàcí kávə̀ I see my head ... listen here for tones. NPs of some length ... Kàná ká nan tsulai kàdíshai all high tones here. ... all the poss prns have same tonal pattern ... *má ← does not like (H) tone here ... super high! does not like má ... móngòrô ìmóngòrô mango [Note the tonal pattern]
tone_statements.locator: item 2015-05.023 (marginal notes beside tone-marked forms); last two fragments item 2015-05.024
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Raw session notes: H (acute), L (grave), some circumflex, 'super high' and 'mid?' queries; tonal minimal pair probed; 'sort of sounds downstepped' tentative. No inventory stated. At least 150 forms.

sources.note: Sec. 3.3 (pp. 9-11) gives Kambari research history and naming; sec. 4.3 'Kambari' phonology subsections (Cicipu, Salka, Auna, TsuVadi) are empty stubs.
